summary.title: The Product-Minded Engineer: The importance of good errors and warnings
summary.one_liner: Good error and warning messages are a high-leverage product interface; learn to categorize errors by audience and raise them at the API/UI boundary with actionable advice.
takeaways: Diagnostics (errors and warnings) are often the primary interface users experience, so they deserve deliberate design.
Categorize each error by audience (end user vs. developer, internal vs. external) and whether it is actionable at runtime or only during development.
Good messages state what happened in the product's terms and tell the user what they can do about it, ideally with suggestions or links.
Raise errors at the API or UI boundary, where the user's intent is known, either via upfront validation or by repackaging lower-level errors with chained exceptions.
summary.summary: This Pragmatic Engineer newsletter issue introduces the O'Reilly book "The Product-Minded Engineer" by Drew Hoskins, including an interview with the author and an excerpt from Chapter 3 on errors and warnings. The excerpt argues that diagnostics are a primary product interface and that errors should be categorized by audience (human or programmer) and actionability. It uses a fictional workplace-chat API, Channelz, to show how to write actionable messages, validate upfront, and repackage lower-level errors at the interface layer. The examples are in Python.
